timeline.text: A neighbourhood library in Hangzhou is trying a new way to help residents repair small household items. Alongside its books, the library now lends basic tools, including screwdrivers and bicycle pumps. The service began after staff noticed that many residents wanted to repair things but did not own the right equipment. Buying a tool for a single repair seemed wasteful, especially for people living in small flats.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: Residents can borrow a kit for three days with their library card. They must first watch a short safety video, but there is no lending fee. During the first month, bicycle pumps were borrowed more often than any other item. Staff had expected screwdrivers to be the most popular. The library is now collecting suggestions before buying more equipment.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: It will not lend electric tools at this stage, because staff say those require more careful training. A weekly repair session is also planned, although volunteers will teach residents basic skills rather than take broken items away for repair.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: Question 1. Why did the library introduce the tool-lending service?

timeline.text: A vegetable market in Chengdu has changed its morning delivery arrangements following complaints from nearby residents. Delivery vehicles previously arrived at different times before sunrise, and drivers often left their engines running while waiting for space. The market has now introduced booked delivery periods and a marked waiting area away from the residential buildings. Drivers must switch off their engines while waiting.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: The change was tested for two weeks. According to the market manager, the number of noise complaints fell, while the average time needed to unload a vehicle remained almost unchanged. Some traders had worried that scheduled deliveries would make fresh vegetables arrive too late, but the booking system allowed them to choose earlier periods when necessary.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: The market will continue the arrangement for another month before deciding whether to make it permanent. The manager said the next step was to improve signs at the entrance, since several first-time drivers had entered the wrong lane. No increase in delivery charges has been announced.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: Question 3. What problem was the market trying to address?
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: Question 4. What happened during the two-week trial?

timeline.text: Students at a university in Wuhan have completed a study of the drinking-water stations on their campus. For four weeks, volunteers counted visits at different times of day and asked users about their experience. The busiest station was close to the sports ground, but it was not the one receiving the most complaints. That was a station near the library, where the narrow space made queues difficult to organise.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: Instead of immediately buying more machines, the university will first move the library station into a wider entrance area. Clear signs will separate people filling bottles from those waiting to enter the building. The students also recommended displaying the date of the latest maintenance check, because some users wanted more information about water quality. The university accepted this suggestion.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: A second survey is planned after the change has been in place for a month. Volunteers will compare waiting times rather than simply count total visits, so they can see whether the new arrangement has actually made the station easier to use.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you are going to hear.

timeline.text: I've brought the draft plan for our community sound exhibition. You suggested recording the old railway station, but I'm worried that we'll spend most of our time travelling.
timeline.speaker: woman

timeline.text: That's fair. We only have three weeks, and the station is nearly two hours away. What about the morning market near campus?
timeline.speaker: man

timeline.text: I like that. But we should avoid recording private conversations. We can ask traders whether they are willing to describe their work, and record the general background separately.
timeline.speaker: woman

timeline.text: Agreed. I'll prepare a short permission form.
timeline.speaker: man

timeline.text: Our tutor said a clear purpose matters more than expensive equipment for this project. We can use the small recorder I've already learned to operate. Let's make a trial recording first.
timeline.speaker: woman

timeline.text: Good. We could visit on Friday morning, then listen to the recording back here. If the wind is too strong, we can try recording under the covered entrance.
timeline.speaker: man

timeline.text: Friday won't work for me. I have a laboratory class until noon. Could we go on Saturday? The market is still busy then.
timeline.speaker: woman

timeline.text: Saturday is fine. For the exhibition, I was thinking of displaying photographs next to each sound. Visitors could read a long explanation about the market's history.
timeline.speaker: man

timeline.text: Photographs would help, but let's keep the labels short. We want people to listen carefully, not spend the whole visit reading. A map could show where each sound was recorded.
timeline.speaker: woman

timeline.text: That makes sense. I'll contact the market office today and ask about permission. Could you draw the map?
timeline.speaker: man

timeline.text: Yes. After the trial, we can decide which parts tell a clear story. We don't have to use everything we record.
timeline.speaker: woman

timeline.text: You've just finished your first week at the design company. How did it go?
timeline.speaker: man

timeline.text: I still get nervous, but that wasn't the main difficulty. I spent too long improving small details before checking whether I had understood the task. On Wednesday, I discovered I had designed the wrong kind of poster.
timeline.speaker: woman

timeline.text: That sounds frustrating. Was the instruction unclear?
timeline.speaker: man

timeline.text: It was short, and I made an assumption instead of asking. My supervisor said a rough sketch shown early would have prevented the mistake. She wasn't expecting a finished design that afternoon.
timeline.speaker: woman

timeline.text: So you need to check the direction before polishing the work.
timeline.speaker: man

timeline.text: Exactly. We agreed that I would send a simple outline at the start of each new task. She'll tell me whether I'm on the right track.
timeline.speaker: woman

timeline.text: Did you work late to replace the poster?
timeline.speaker: man

timeline.text: Not that night. The deadline was Friday, so I still had Thursday to correct it. She wanted me to understand why the design was needed.
timeline.speaker: woman

timeline.text: That's useful advice. What will you do next week?
timeline.speaker: man

timeline.text: Help the team prepare a small exhibition. My job is to check whether visitors can follow the signs between rooms. I'll walk through the building with someone who has never been there.
timeline.speaker: woman

timeline.text: Will you ask that person to explain where they feel uncertain?
timeline.speaker: man

timeline.text: Yes, without telling them the correct route first. If I guide them the whole way, the signs may seem clearer than they really are.
timeline.speaker: woman

timeline.text: It sounds as if your first week changed how you think about good design.
timeline.speaker: man

timeline.text: It did. Looking attractive is important, but a design also has to work for the people using it.
timeline.speaker: woman

timeline.text: Questions 16 to 18 are based on the passage you are going to hear.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: When a university repair group first invited students to bring in broken belongings, the organisers expected the main challenge to be finding enough tools. On the first afternoon, however, they discovered a different problem. Many visitors handed over an item and immediately reached for their phones. They expected the volunteers to complete the repair for them. The group decided that this approach did not match its educational purpose.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: At the next meeting, every visitor was asked to stay at the table and take part. Volunteers began by asking what had happened before the item stopped working. They then explained one possible cause and invited the owner to carry out a safe, simple check. Anything involving dangerous electrical work was referred to a professional service. Repairs sometimes took longer under the new arrangement.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: Yet students began to describe the sessions differently. Instead of saying that someone had fixed a lamp, they explained how they had found a loose connection or why a part needed replacing. The organisers do not measure success only by the number of completed repairs. They also ask visitors what they learned and whether they would feel comfortable making a similar check at home.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: The group has kept its small size so that volunteers have time to explain. It cannot repair every item, and safety checks are never skipped.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: Question 16. What unexpected problem did the organisers discover?
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: Question 17. How did the group change its sessions?
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: Question 18. What does the group consider a sign of success?
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: Questions 19 to 21 are based on the passage you are going to hear.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: A student team producing a weekly science podcast used to believe that every episode needed as much information as possible. Members collected facts from several sources and prepared long scripts. Comments suggested that the programme was difficult to follow while walking or travelling on a bus. The team initially blamed the sound quality. They bought a better microphone, yet the listening figures changed very little.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: A teacher then asked them to describe the purpose of one episode in a single sentence. Each team member gave a different answer. The difficulty was not simply technical: the programme lacked a clear central question. For the next episode, the team chose one question about how a familiar household object worked. They kept only the information needed to answer it.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: A short example came before the technical term, and a brief summary appeared at the end. The episode was shorter, but a greater proportion of listeners reached the final minute. The students now ask someone outside the team to listen to a draft. Rather than asking only whether it sounds interesting, they ask that person to explain the main idea afterwards. If the explanation is confused, they revise the structure before adding any more facts.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: They still check information carefully and provide sources in the programme notes. Reducing the amount of information has not meant reducing their responsibility for accuracy.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: Question 19. What complaint did listeners make about the original podcast?
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: Question 20. What did the teacher's question reveal?
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: Question 21. What do the students now ask an outside listener to do?
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: At the beginning of summer, students at a college noticed that the shortest route between the library and the bus stop was not always the most comfortable. At midday, a wide paved square had very little shade. A student geography group decided to map the shade along several walking routes. Members visited each route in the morning, at midday and in the late afternoon. They recorded where shade fell along each path.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: They soon found that a route described as shady in the morning could be almost entirely exposed a few hours later. The first version of their map used a single green line for comfortable routes. After showing it to classmates, the group changed the design. The new version lets readers choose a time of day and compare alternative paths. The college has used the observations to identify a small number of places where temporary shade could help.
timeline.speaker: narrator

timeline.text: Before making permanent changes, staff plan to count how people use those areas. The students have also added a date to the map and will update it as the season changes. They explain that shade depends on the sun's position and the growth of trees, so a useful map needs careful, regular revision. Their aim is to make daily choices easier while giving planners evidence about where improvements would matter most.
timeline.speaker: narrator
